name: Trade secret contamination
blurb: Cover against claims that internal source code leaked into a public training set.
summary: Cover against claims that internal source code leaked into a public training set.

part_3_high_value_red_flags: Broad intellectual property exclusions that carve out all trade secret, copyright, and patent claims, leaving no coverage for the core exposure.
Data breach or cyber exclusions that treat the leak of internal source code into a public training set as an excluded unauthorized access event rather than a covered error.
Prior acts or retroactive date restrictions that exclude claims arising from code leaked before the policy inception, which is common for long tail contamination.
Sublimits for intellectual property claims that are far below the potential defense costs of a multi party trade secret misappropriation suit.
Exclusions for loss of trade secret or diminution in value of proprietary information, which would bar coverage for the insured's own losses if the policy is intended to include first party coverage.
Contractual liability exclusions that remove coverage for indemnity obligations owed to data contributors or downstream users.
Known loss or prior knowledge exclusions that could be triggered if the insured was aware of the leak before binding coverage.
manuscript_wording_and_carve_backs: Delete the intellectual property exclusion and replace it with a specific carve back for trade secret misappropriation arising from the insured's handling of training data.
Add a definition of contaminated training data that includes internal source code leaked into a public training set, and confirm coverage for resulting third party claims.
Negotiate a contractual liability extension that covers indemnity obligations to data contributors and downstream users for trade secret contamination.
Remove any prior acts exclusion for trade secret claims, or set a retroactive date that aligns with the insured's first use of public training data.
Add a sublimit for defense costs outside the limit of liability for trade secret claims, as these suits are defense heavy and can exhaust limits quickly.
Include a data recall or data remediation endorsement that covers the cost of removing contaminated code from public training sets and notifying affected parties.
Ensure the definition of claim includes regulatory investigations and pre suit demands related to trade secret contamination, not just formal lawsuits.

part_4_program_structure_and_limits.bi_waiting_period: Business interruption from trade secret contamination would typically have a waiting period of 30 to 60 days, reflecting the time needed to detect the leak and quantify the impact on revenue or model performance.
part_4_program_structure_and_limits.business_interruption: Business interruption coverage should be negotiated on a manuscript basis to include loss of income from model retraining, reputational harm, and loss of trade secret value, as standard BI forms do not contemplate intangible data contamination.
part_4_program_structure_and_limits.property_eb_equipment: Electronic data processing equipment coverage is not relevant to trade secret contamination unless the leak causes physical damage to servers, which is unlikely, so this should be excluded or sublimited to avoid premium misallocation.
part_4_program_structure_and_limits.per_occurrence_primary_excess_layered_pr: This exposure is not property damage based, so property layers are not the primary driver; instead, the program should be built on a technology E&O primary with per claim limits, and excess layers should follow that form.

part_2_paper_type_and_limit_structure.cgl_primary: A commercial general liability policy would not respond to pure financial loss from trade secret misappropriation, so the primary layer should be a technology errors and omissions or cyber liability policy with specific intellectual property coverage.
part_2_paper_type_and_limit_structure.paper_basis: Claims made, because trade secret contamination claims often surface years after the leak when the contaminated model is deployed or audited, and the insured needs coverage tied to when the claim is first made rather than when the leak occurred.
part_2_paper_type_and_limit_structure.excess_umbrella_towers: Excess layers should follow form over the technology E&O primary and include dedicated limits for intellectual property and data contamination claims, as standard umbrella policies often exclude trade secret and IP exposures.

part_1_core_third_party_liability_exposu: Claims by a third party that its trade secret source code was incorporated into the insured's public training set without authorization, constituting misappropriation.
Claims by downstream users of the public training set that they inadvertently incorporated the leaked code into their own products and now face infringement or misappropriation suits.
Breach of confidentiality claims from contributors or partners who supplied code under non disclosure agreements that the insured failed to honor.
Negligence claims alleging the insured failed to implement reasonable safeguards to prevent internal source code from entering public training data.
Contractual indemnity claims from customers or data providers who relied on the insured's representations that the training set was free of proprietary code.
Regulatory actions alleging failure to protect trade secrets under data protection or unfair competition laws.
Defamation or business disparagement claims if the insured publicly identifies the source of the leaked code and that identification is challenged.

underwriter_wants_to_know: What controls exist to prevent internal source code from being included in public training datasets, such as code scanning and data provenance checks.
Whether the insured has contractual warranties from data contributors that their submissions do not contain trade secrets or proprietary code.
How the insured detects and responds to reports of contaminated training data, including takedown and model retraining procedures.
The volume and sensitivity of internal source code that could plausibly be exposed through public training set ingestion.
Whether the insured has any prior incidents of trade secret leakage into public datasets or related litigation.
The jurisdictions where the public training set is accessible, as trade secret law varies significantly by country.
The insured's insurance history for intellectual property and technology errors and omissions claims.
